readerTitle: A blog post promises 3x sales. Two questions to ask first.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (대기업 소프트웨어 회사의 고객성공팀, 상업용 청소 B2B 업체) + 실제 연구 (노인 점화 연구와 재현 실패, Many Labs 앵커링 재현)
insight: '심리학 해킹' 글은 '재현됐는가'와 '실험실 밖에서도 통했는가' 두 질문으로 걸러, 통과한 정도에 따라 '도입·작은 테스트·거절' 중 하나를 고른다.
misconception: 연구를 인용한 글이면 믿을 만하고, 유명한 효과일수록 우리 고객에게도 그대로 통한다. 반대로 재현 실패 소식을 들으면 심리학 연구는 전부 쓸모없다고 여긴다.

sources.text: Bargh, J. A., Chen, M., & Burrows, L. (1996). Automaticity of social behavior. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 71(2).
Doyen, S., Klein, O., Pichon, C.-L., & Cleeremans, A. (2012). Behavioral priming: It's all in the mind, but whose mind? PLoS ONE, 7(1).
Klein, R. A., et al. (2014). Investigating variation in replicability: A "Many Labs" replication project. Social Psychology, 45(3).
블로그 글, 수치(3배, 21%), 업체는 모두 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Bargh 외(1996): 노인 관련 단어로 점화된 학생들이 실험 후 더 천천히 걸었다는 보고. 연도와 내용을 원문으로 확인하세요.
Doyen 외(2012, PLoS ONE): 적외선 센서로 보행 시간을 측정한 재현 시도에서 효과를 찾지 못함. 카드의 'more careful timing' 표현이 정확한지 확인하세요.
Many Labs 1(Klein 외, 2014): 여러 나라 36개 표본에서 앵커링 효과가 강하게 재현됨. 카드의 'dozens of labs', 'in 2014' 표현을 확인하세요. 해당 앵커링 과제는 숫자 추정형 문제였다는 점(실제 구매 결정이 아님)도 확인하세요.
3번 카드의 인용 사슬(60명 학생, 가상 제안)과 8번 카드의 빨간 버튼 +21%는 실제 연구나 기업 사례가 아닌 가상 설정입니다. 실제 사례로 오해되지 않도록 illustrative 표시를 유지하세요.

cards.title: Seven psychology hacks, one Slack message
body: A link lands in your team channel: *7 Psychology Hacks That Triple Conversions*. Your director adds one line: "Can we try all seven this quarter?"
Each hack cites a study. Some may help. Some never worked outside a classroom. This lesson is about telling them apart in ten minutes.

image.label: A phone showing a hack listicle in a team chat
image.brief: 사무실 책상 위 휴대폰 화면에 팀 채팅창. 링크 미리보기에 "7 Psychology Hacks That Triple Conversions" 제목과 반짝이는 뇌 아이콘. 옆에 돋보기를 든 손. 실제 메신저 앱 로고나 UI는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Hack #3 promises 3x sign-ups.
body: You run the customer success team inside a large software company. Hack #3 says: add a countdown timer to renewal offers. "A study found urgency tripled sign-ups."
Before anyone builds it, what do you check first?

options.text: Who was in the study, and were they spending real money?
options.feedback: This is *lab results in the real world*. A choice made by students for course credit may not survive a busy customer with a budget. One click on the citation often answers it.

options.text: How many other companies recommend it
options.feedback: Popularity shows a claim spreads well, not that it works. Hack posts copy each other, so ten mentions can trace back to one study.

options.text: Nothing yet. Just A/B test it
options.feedback: Testing beats guessing, but it costs engineering time and renewals if it backfires. A two-minute source check tells you whether the test is worth running.

cards.title: The 3x shrank at every link.

breakdown.label: The hack post
breakdown.detail: Cites another blog, not a study

cards.callout: This doesn't prove urgency is useless. It proves the 3x is a story, not a measurement of *your* renewals.
cards.softwareNote: In software, the sticking point is that a renewal is a budget decision, often made by someone other than the daily user. A student clicking an imaginary offer faces none of that.

cards.title: Two questions from this unit
body: Most hack posts fail one of these. Many fail both.
list: **Did it replicate?** Has anyone else, ideally a larger independent team, found the same effect? (*When famous findings don't replicate*)
**Did it leave the lab?** Were the people real customers, making real decisions, with real money and real distractions? (*Lab results in the real world*)
cards.callout: Pass both: worth a test. Pass one: a small, cheap test. Pass neither: a polite no.
cards.softwareNote: For a growth team, these two questions are a cheap filter before the backlog. They decide which hacks earn an experiment slot and which never reach engineering.

cards.title: Famous isn't the same as solid.
body: In 1996, a well-known study reported that students primed with words about old age walked more slowly afterward. It became a staple of persuasion books.

In 2012, another team repeated it with more careful timing and did not find the effect. Meanwhile anchoring, the pull of a first number, held up strongly when dozens of labs re-ran it together in 2014.
The lesson isn't "psychology is fake." It's that **each claim needs its own check**.

image.label: Two study cards: one cracked, one solid
image.brief: 두 장의 연구 카드. 왼쪽 "Priming: walking speed" 카드는 금이 가 있고 "Not replicated" 도장. 오른쪽 "Anchoring" 카드는 여러 겹 쌓여 단단해 보이고 "Replicated" 도장. 플랫 일러스트, 실제 학술지 로고 없음.

cards.title: An anchoring hack for sales proposals
body: You run sales at a commercial cleaning firm that bids for office contracts. A blog post says: open every proposal with your premium package, because anchoring makes buyers pay more.

options.text: Put it in every proposal from Monday. Anchoring is well proven
options.feedback: It passes *did it replicate?*. But those tests mostly asked people to guess numbers, not facilities managers comparing three bids. A full rollout bets your win rate on that gap.

options.text: Skip it. Most psychology hacks don't hold up
options.feedback: Skepticism protects you from weak hacks, but this one passed the replication check. Rejecting it outright skips a cheap idea with decent evidence.

options.text: Try it on the next 20 proposals and compare deal size and win rate
options.feedback: Replication earned it a test. A small trial answers *did it leave the lab?* for your own buyers, at little risk.

cards.title: Your own test can fool you too.
body: Small tests throw up flukes. Twenty proposals can swing on one large client. Treat an early win as a reason to keep testing, not as proof.
And evidence is not permission. A countdown timer might work and still be a fake deadline. Whether a tactic is **honest** is a separate question from whether it's real.

cards.title: "One company's test: red buttons, +21%."
body: Back at the software company, your director forwards another post. A retailer changed its checkout button from green to red and reported 21% more sales.
How should your team read it?

options.text: Real customers, real money. It's proven
options.feedback: It left the lab, but it never replicated. One page, one season, one audience leaves plenty of room for a fluke or a hidden cause.

options.text: A real-world clue that hasn't replicated. Worth a cheap test, not a redesign
options.feedback: You used both questions. It passes *did it leave the lab?* and fails *did it replicate?*, which is exactly the profile of something to test small.

options.text: It's not peer-reviewed, so ignore it
options.feedback: Fair caution, but company tests can be useful clues. The real gap is replication, not the missing journal.

cards.title: Two questions turn a hack post into a short list.
body: **Concepts used:** *When famous findings don't replicate* and *Lab results in the real world*. Pass both: test it. Pass one: test it small. Pass neither: say no.
**Try it today:** open the last business article you read that cited a study. Click through. Who were the people, and has anyone repeated it?
